questions.q: In which year did Constantine issue the Edict of Milan granting religious tolerance to Christians, and what immediate political crisis preceded it?
questions.a: 313 CE; the Edict followed Constantine's victory at the Battle of the Milvian Bridge (312 CE) against Maxentius, during a civil war for control of the Western Empire. A wrong answer (e.g., 325 CE — Council of Nicaea) reveals confusion between legalisation and doctrinal standardisation; a wrong date like 380 CE confuses Constantine with Theodosius.

questions.q: Why did Paul's decision to preach to Gentiles without requiring circumcision or dietary laws prove decisive for Christianity's expansion across the Roman Empire?
questions.a: It removed ethnic and ritual barriers, allowing Christianity to become a universal (katholikos) religion accessible to any Roman citizen or provincial, unlike Judaism which remained ethnically bound. A wrong answer focusing only on "Paul travelled a lot" misses the theological breakthrough; an answer citing "Roman roads" confuses infrastructure with the internal logic of the faith's adaptability.

questions.q: A historian argues: "Christianity spread because the Roman Empire was collapsing and people needed hope." Using evidence from the 2nd and 3rd centuries CE, evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is partially true but reverses chronology: Christianity grew rapidly during the Pax Romana (2nd century) when the empire was stable, not just during the 3rd-century crisis. Evidence: Pliny's letters (c. 112 CE) show Christians in Bithynia under Trajan; the faith spread via trade networks and urban centres before the Crisis of the Third Century. A wrong answer accepting the claim wholesale ignores the 150-year growth phase before severe instability; it also neglects the organisational strength of bishoprics that predated the crisis.

questions.q: Compare the role of Constantine (312–337 CE) in Christianity's rise with Ashoka (268–232 BCE) in Buddhism's spread. Identify two structural similarities and one critical difference in their methods.
questions.a: Similarities: (1) Both used imperial patronage to build sacred architecture (Constantine: St. Peter's, Holy Sepulchre; Ashoka: stupas, pillars) and (2) both convened councils to define orthodoxy (Nicaea 325 CE; Third Buddhist Council 250 BCE). Difference: Ashoka promoted dhamma as a universal ethical code without enforcing Buddhism as a state religion, whereas Constantine progressively favoured Christianity legally and fiscally, culminating in Theodosius's establishment. A wrong answer equating both as "state religion imposition" misreads Ashoka's edicts which explicitly respect all sects.

questions.q: Assess the argument that Diocletian's Great Persecution (303–311 CE) strengthened rather than weakened the Christian church. Support your judgement with two pieces of evidence.
questions.a: The persecution inadvertently strengthened the church by: (1) creating a cult of martyrs that enhanced group cohesion and attracted converts seeking meaning in suffering (e.g., Perpetua and Felicity in Carthage), and (2) forcing the church to develop a more resilient, hierarchical episcopal structure to survive clandestine operation. A wrong answer claiming "persecution always destroys movements" ignores the sociological pattern where moderate repression increases commitment; a wrong answer citing only "Constantine ended it" misses the internal transformation during the persecution decade.

questions.q: Construct a 6-event annotated timeline (30–380 CE) showing the turning points in Christianity's legal status, labelling each as "persecution," "tolerance," "patronage," or "establishment."
questions.a: Expected timeline: 30 CE (Crucifixion — persecution context), 64 CE (Nero's persecution — persecution), 112 CE (Pliny-Trajan correspondence — persecution), 250 CE (Decian edict — persecution), 303 CE (Diocletian's Great Persecution — persecution), 313 CE (Edict of Milan — tolerance), 325 CE (Council of Nicaea — patronage), 380 CE (Edict of Thessalonica — establishment). A poor answer lists only councils or emperors without legal-status labels, or omits the 150-year gap between Nero and Decius, showing weak chronological reasoning.
